title: Charge, current, p.d.
examples: What is the difference between charge and current?
How do I draw a simple circuit diagram?
Can you explain what potential difference really means?

explain.say: Today we are learning about electricity basics. We will look at charge, current, and potential difference. These ideas help us understand how electricity flows.
Electric charge is the basic property of matter. It comes in two types, positive and negative. We measure charge using a unit called the coulomb.
Electric current is the flow of electric charge. Think of it like water flowing in a pipe. We measure current in amperes, or amps.
Potential difference is the work done per unit charge. It is the push that makes the charge move. We measure this in volts.
Finally, we use symbols for circuits. A cell is shown as a long line and a short line. A resistor is shown as a zig-zag line.

faq.q: What is the difference between charge and current?
faq.a: Charge is the total amount of electric stuff. Current is how fast that charge is moving over time. You might also ask about the flow rate of charge.
asks: What is the difference between Q and I?
Is current the same as charge?
How is current related to charge?

faq.q: What does potential difference actually measure?
faq.a: Potential difference measures the energy difference between two points. It is the electrical 'push' that makes the current flow. Sometimes people ask about the voltage or work done per charge.
asks: What is voltage in simple terms?
Does potential difference mean the same as energy?
What is the unit for potential difference?

faq.q: Why do we need circuit symbols?
faq.a: Circuit symbols give a standard way to draw electrical circuits. This way helps everyone understand the diagram quickly. You could also ask how to draw a circuit or what the symbols mean.
asks: How do I draw a circuit diagram?

faq.q: Is the current always measured in amps?
faq.a: Yes, the standard unit for electric current is the ampere, or amp. This unit measures the rate of charge flow. You could also ask what the unit for current is.
asks: What is the unit for electric current?
Can current be measured in something else?

faq.q: If I change the voltage, does the current change?
faq.a: Yes, generally a higher potential difference causes a larger current. This relationship is key to understanding circuits. You might wonder about the relationship between V and I.
asks: Is there a link between potential difference and current?
If I increase V, what happens to I?

facts: Electric charge is measured in coulombs, symbol Q.
Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes, symbol I.
Potential difference is work done per unit charge, measured in volts, symbol V.
A cell symbol shows a long line and a short line.

quiz.say: Which quantity is measured in volts?
quiz.why: Potential difference is defined as work done divided by charge, and its unit is the volt. Mistakes might confuse it with current (amperes) or charge (coulombs).

wrong.0: Watts measure power, which is energy used per time.
wrong.2: Amperes measure current, which is charge flow over time.
wrong.3: Coulombs measure the total amount of electric charge.

quiz.say: If a charge of six coulombs passes in ten seconds, what is the current?
quiz.why: Current equals charge divided by time, so six divided by ten is zero point six amperes. Mistakes might incorrectly multiply the values or use the wrong formula.

wrong.0: This option leaves the division in a fraction format instead of calculating the decimal value.
wrong.2: This option incorrectly multiplies the charge and time values.
wrong.3: This option forgets to divide by the time taken.

quiz.say: Which symbol correctly represents a resistor in a circuit diagram?
quiz.why: The standard symbol for a resistor is a zig-zag line. Mistakes might confuse it with the battery symbol or other components.

wrong.0: This symbol usually represents a light bulb or a general component.
wrong.1: Two parallel lines often represent connecting wires.
wrong.2: This symbol represents the power source, like a cell.
